blocks.text: For two Availability Zones, check both address fit and usable capacity. Complete the external IP-addressing and CIDR preparation first.
An IPv4 subnet CIDR must be within its VPC CIDR and must not overlap another subnet in that VPC.

tiles.title: Define recovery time and recovery point objectives
tiles.summary: Derive RTO and RPO from business requirements. Compare recovery capabilities with both restoration-time and time-based data-loss limits.

blocks.text: Name tolerated downtime and tolerated data loss separately; they are different business requirements.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption.
Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Set recovery objectives from business requirements and use them to choose recovery capabilities that meet the tolerated downtime and data loss.

blocks.caption: Business recovery limits and candidate capabilities

blocks.text: Compare each recovery approach with both business limits in the table. Meeting restoration time while losing too much recent data fails the data-loss requirement. Recent data alone does not establish timely restoration. These are illustrative business limits, not recommended AWS defaults.
RTO bounds restoration time; RPO bounds data loss measured in time. Neither substitutes for the other.

With RDS, AWS manages database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance, while customers manage their data and application use.
Assign duties by the service boundary: AWS manages its infrastructure, while customers retain responsibilities for data, access and customer-controlled configuration.

Interpret the supplied EC2 OS-update report as customer guest-OS work and the supplied RDS parameter-check report as customer-controlled database configuration; RDS parameter groups contain database engine configuration values.

tiles.title: Distinguish capacity requirements from availability requirements
tiles.summary: Match capacity to demand. Separately evaluate independent surviving capacity for a component-failure constraint; equal totals do not settle availability.

blocks.text: Separate ordinary demand from the service requirement after a component fails.
Redundant components and multiple locations can keep a workload available when a component fails.
Capacity must accommodate workload demand; adding or removing resources helps match capacity to changing demand.
For a component-failure constraint, evaluate independent redundant capacity rather than merely increasing the size of the same component.

blocks.text: Both proposals have equal total capacity. Evaluate that capacity against ordinary demand, then evaluate independent surviving capacity against the post-loss service requirement. A larger single component can address demand without answering the failure requirement.

tiles.title: Evaluate an IAM identity policy for a requested operation after external access-control preparation
tiles.summary: Match action, resource and conditions to identity-policy statements. Applicable explicit deny overrides allow; no applicable allow means implicit deny.

blocks.text: Evaluate the requested action and resource, not whether the policy looks permissive. Complete the external access-control preparation first.
An identity-based policy attaches to an identity and specifies permitted or denied actions on resources.
A statement uses Effect, Action and Resource, with optional Condition tests to scope when it applies.
For a request, compare action, resource and condition values with applicable statements; explicit deny overrides an allow, and absent an applicable allow the request is implicitly denied.

blocks.caption: Object-read requests matched to identity-policy statements

blocks.text: Compare the object-read request with Action, Resource and Condition. An unmet condition or unmatched resource can leave no applicable allow: implicit deny. When an applicable Deny also covers the request, it overrides the Allow. The supplied table evaluates these identity-policy rules, not every AWS policy type.
An Allow elsewhere does not allow this request. Scope and conditions must match; applicable explicit deny wins.

tiles.title: Interpret DORA delivery and recovery evidence
tiles.summary: Compare deployment frequency and change lead time with change fail rate and failed deployment recovery time. Interpret all four over time within application context, not as individual rankings.

blocks.text: Read throughput and instability together before interpreting a delivery report.
Deployment frequency measures how often changes are deployed; change lead time measures the elapsed time for a committed change to reach production.
Change fail rate measures the proportion of deployments requiring intervention; failed deployment recovery time measures how long recovery from a failed deployment takes.
Compare throughput and instability measures together over time and within application context rather than using one measure to rank individuals.

For the same application, more deployments and shorter commit-to-production time concern throughput. A greater proportion needing intervention concerns change fail rate; recovery duration supplies the other instability measure. Keep all four measures together across reporting periods, rather than ranking individuals by one improving measure.
Frequent delivery alone does not describe stability. Interpret the combined evidence within application context.

blocks.caption: Orders delivery throughput and instability over two periods

tiles.summary: Patterns constrain named fields to acceptable values. Omitted fields need not match. Test matching and nonmatching samples before using a pattern in a rule.

Write a JSON object containing the fields to filter and arrays of acceptable values; fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match.
Test a pattern against both matching and nonmatching sample events with the EventBridge sandbox or TestEventPattern before using it in a rule.

annotations.text: Constrain source and detail-type to arrays of acceptable values.
Positive sample: both constrained values satisfy the pattern. id is omitted from the pattern.
Negative sample: detail-type differs from its acceptable value.
Only id changes from the positive sample. Because id is omitted, the matching decision is unchanged.

blocks.text: The pattern accepts source lab.orders and detail-type OrderReady. Test those values, then test a sample with detail-type OrderCancelled. Also vary an omitted field: it is not required to match. Compare test results with the intended requirement before using a rule; these names are invented sample data.
An event need not duplicate every field of a sample. Omitted fields are not required to match; positive and negative tests expose the boundary.

remediation_steps.title: Separate the two kinds of evidence

blocks.text: An EventBridge event pattern describes event fields and values that an event must match.
Write a JSON object containing the fields to filter and arrays of acceptable values; fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match.
Test a pattern against both matching and nonmatching sample events with the EventBridge sandbox or TestEventPattern before using it in a rule.
